title_vi: Big endian và little endian: thứ tự byte trong bộ nhớ

claims.claim_vi: The source names little endian, big endian and the question why byte order matters when data moves between systems. Only the names and the question are reused; the source's PowerPC, Motorola 68k and file storage statements are not repeated because the primary documents read do not contain them.
claims.verified_by: Source body read from the pinned commit; the statement is in the source text.

claims.claim_vi: Python struct documentation: the number 1023 (0x3ff) is 03 ff in big-endian and ff 03 in little-endian, and struct.pack('>h', 1023) and struct.pack('<h', 1023) give those bytes.
claims.verified_by: Read from a raw copy at the pinned commit in the URL (a later change to the default branch does not alter it).

claims.claim_vi: Python struct documentation: native byte order depends on the host system; Intel x86, AMD64 (x86-64) and Apple M1 are little-endian; IBM z and many legacy architectures are big-endian; sys.byteorder reports the system's byte order.
claims.verified_by: Read from a raw copy at the pinned commit in the URL (a later change to the default branch does not alter it).

claims.claim_vi: Python struct documentation: network byte order is always big-endian, as defined in an IETF RFC the documentation cites (the RFC itself was not read).
claims.verified_by: Read from a raw copy at the pinned commit in the URL (a later change to the default branch does not alter it).

claims.claim_vi: Python struct documentation advice: when exchanging data beyond the process, such as networking or storage, specify the exact byte order, size and alignment and do not assume the native order; network byte order is big-endian while many popular CPUs are little-endian.
claims.verified_by: Read from a raw copy at the pinned commit in the URL (a later change to the default branch does not alter it).

claims.claim_vi: Linux byteorder/generic.h comment: htonl, htons, ntohl and ntohs convert long and short integers between network and host format.
claims.verified_by: Read from a raw copy at the pinned commit in the URL (a later change to the default branch does not alter it).

claims.claim_vi: Reading ff 03 as a big-endian unsigned two-byte integer gives 0xff03 = 65283 (computed by the author).
claims.verified_by: Author's general knowledge; not checked against primary documentation.

claims.claim_vi: Byte order concerns the order of bytes of a number, not of bits within a byte; the glosses of IBM, AMD and IETF.
claims.verified_by: Author's general knowledge; not checked against primary documentation.

design_notes_vi: Hai chuỗi hai bước cho big và little endian với số 1023, nơi dùng (theo tài liệu Python), ba điều cần nhớ. Ví dụ lấy từ tài liệu Python thay vì tự nghĩ. Không dùng ảnh nguồn.
source_deviations: Source has three short sections and no worked example; the lesson keeps the names and the question why byte order matters, and explains them with the 1023 example, the machine list and the advice of the Python struct documentation and a Linux header comment instead of translating the source sentences.

Source says older PowerPC and Motorola 68k are often big endian and that file storage uses big endian; the documents read do not say so, so the lesson drops both and names the machines the Python documentation names (Intel x86, AMD64, Apple M1, IBM z).
Source does not mention that byte order is distinct from bit order or give a mixed-endian failure case; the lesson adds the check question as the author's computation.
editorial_note_vi: Bài mới viết trong kho này, chờ review kỹ thuật. Phần giải thích dựa vào tài liệu Python struct và một tệp của nhân Linux ở commit cố định; chuẩn của IETF mà tài liệu Python dẫn chưa được đọc trực tiếp, và phép tính 65283 cùng giải nghĩa viết tắt là của người biên soạn.
